question: What product capabilities appear to be most important to prospects?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every product capability, feature, integration or connector that the prospect asks about, requests, praises, or names as a requirement or concern, including any stated priority, urgency, or deal-blocking need, and quote the prospect's wording where possible.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as new business prospects, so call_types set to Prospect only.
No specific company named, so companies is empty.
'Most important' cannot be seen from a single call, so the reader is asked for the underlying statements about needs and priorities for later aggregation.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.
findings.context: Prospect wants a workflow layer that moves work along and makes ownership visible, not another dashboard. — Core capability priority stated at the start of discovery.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.
findings.context: Prospect needs operational telemetry and visibility into why workflows failed and whether failures repeat. — Pain point around observability of cross-system processes.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The happy path is not the hard part. Anyone can demo the happy path.
findings.context: Prospect requires exception handling and failure behavior tested beyond the happy path: missing data, API timeouts, approver inaction, mid-workflow state changes. — Rachel set a condition for evaluating the product.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.
findings.context: Prospect wants exception queues owned by a team rather than a named individual, with run history visible to admins. — Tom identified individual ownership as a cause of current breakage; OrbitFlow said team routing is supported.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
findings.context: Prospect wants schema-change and bad-data detection, since integrations previously failed silently after field renames or picklist changes. — Concern about silent failure in current automations.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems, because that's where context goes missing.
findings.context: Salesforce connector reliability is the deal-breaker; Slack and data systems matter next for phase one; Gainsight is useful but not essential. — Integration priority ranking in response to OrbitFlow's question.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Can we get metrics out into our own monitoring? I don't want operationally critical automation only visible inside a vendor console.
findings.context: Prospect wants run logs, metrics and failures exportable to their own monitoring and incident tooling rather than visible only in a vendor console. — Tom said this matters more than a dashboard.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?
findings.context: Prospect requires version history and visibility into what changed in a workflow, plus change-management scenarios in the evaluation. — Concern about breaking changes made without review.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Can we see the prompt and the model config? And can we switch AI off entirely for a workspace?
findings.context: Prospect wants controls on AI: ability to inspect prompts and model config, disable AI per workspace, and a written commitment that customer data is not used for training. — AI capability concerns; OrbitFlow said data is not used for training and this belongs in the contract.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We'll have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without necessarily seeing all the customer data in it.
findings.context: Prospect requires permission separation so admins can see step failures without seeing all customer payload data. — Field-level access concern; OrbitFlow said exact field masking should be part of security design.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We need the usual vendor review, SSO, audit logs.
findings.context: Prospect's baseline security requirements are vendor review, SSO and audit logs; SSO and audit logs are part of the usual review, not a deal gate. — Security is quick and not the gating issue for the prospect.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Can secrets be rotated without editing every workflow?
findings.context: Prospect wants workflows to call internal APIs and rotate secrets centrally without editing every workflow. — Technical integration questions asked near end of call.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: identifying renewal risk by combining CRM fields, support activity and product usage signals out of Snowflake. I don't need it now.
findings.context: Prospect wants a bounded phase-one workflow and the architecture to not rule out a later renewal-risk use case combining Snowflake data with CRM signals. — Future use case, explicitly not phase one.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of agentic AI and prefers deterministic rules for high-stakes steps; AI should be optional and explainable. — Concern about explainability of AI features.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Prospect's top gate is a BAA; without one OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow involving protected health information (deal-blocking requirement). — Security architect states this as the gate on the list; security review came first on the call.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: we need to resolve the BAA question, review your subprocessors, SSO and SCIM, understand retention, and confirm how US data is handled.
findings.context: Security architect's requirement list includes SSO and SCIM, subprocessor review, retention, and US data handling. — Opening agenda from the security architect; SSO/SCIM is named as a requirement.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise.
findings.context: Vendor states SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are available, but only on the Enterprise tier. — Vendor baseline capability statement during security review.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: What happens to data sent to an LLM provider?
findings.context: Prospect requires that the AI/LLM feature not be used for phase one; AI steps are acceptable only as a separately reviewed later phase, and the no-training-on-customer-data commitment must be in the contract. — Security concern about LLM provider data handling; prospect accepts deferring AI.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: If it only lives in your console it's not an audit trail, it's a screenshot.
findings.context: Prospect needs audit logs exportable to their own SIEM; console-only logs are not acceptable as an audit trail. — Security requirement; vendor says audit export is on Enterprise and run events are available via APIs and webhooks.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
findings.context: Prospect needs field-level masking so admins can see a step failed without seeing record contents; vendor says this is designable, not a standard checkbox. — Run-data visibility concern; vendor declined to promise it as a yes.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
findings.context: Prospect's core operational pain is weak run history and monitoring of automations; they cannot see which step failed, why, or how often. — Current-state discussion; the need is observability rather than building more automations.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Can I see a failed one?
findings.context: Prospect wants run history and exception handling that shows inputs, steps, and failure points; the vendor demo showed this, and the prospect asked to see a failed run. — Vendor demo of run history and exception queue in response to prospect request.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual?
findings.context: Prospect requires ownership of automations to sit with teams, not named individuals, and wants workflows to survive staff changes. — Governance requirement tied to automations rotting after people leave; vendor says queues can route to groups.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: That's the backlog answer, potentially.
findings.context: Prospect wants reusable components so the systems group builds subflows and business users assemble workflows, reducing the request backlog. — Prospect sees this as the backlog answer; vendor says it compounds over time.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable none of the rest matters.
findings.context: Prospect's phase-one use case needs integrations with HubSpot, Microsoft Teams, Jira Service Management, and Azure AD; Databricks is API-only and not phase one. The system of record connector is the deal-breaker. — Integration priorities; prospect says reliability of the system-of-record connector matters most.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing.
findings.context: Prospect wants workflows that handle missing data, API timeouts, approval delays, and mid-run state changes, and wants a messy-data evaluation. — Reliability requirement; vendor agreed to test with messy data.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: We've had integrations break because someone renamed a field and nothing said anything.
findings.context: Prospect wants alerting and handling for schema changes, since renamed fields have previously broken integrations silently. — Vendor says mapping errors surface on runs and error-rate alerts are possible.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Do you have version history? If someone changes a condition on a Friday and it breaks, can we see what changed?
findings.context: Prospect requires version history and change visibility, plus a change-management scenario in evaluation. — Vendor says version history exists; rollback varies by package.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: In practice it lives or dies on whether the permission model is genuinely least-privilege or just a UI that hides things.
findings.context: Prospect wants a least-privilege permission model for a governed ops-builder use case; they will test it rather than accept a UI that hides things. — Second use case; Elliot's stated concern about permissions, with a follow-up demo agreed.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Complex flows are difficult to monitor.
findings.context: Prospect wants a workflow layer that complements Power Automate, which is already covered by their Microsoft agreement and is hard to monitor for complex flows. — Competitive context; prospect says Power Automate is the real alternative.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Shopify. A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
findings.context: Prospect's most important integration is Shopify; she requires a native, event-driven Shopify trigger and rejects polling. — Prospect names Shopify as the one that 'has to work perfectly'; vendor declined to confirm trigger coverage and promised a written answer.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Can I set an alert on a failure rate rather than an individual failure?
findings.context: Prospect wants automation alerting based on failure rate thresholds rather than per-failure notifications. — Concern about alert fatigue across ~60 automations; vendor confirmed threshold-based error alerting.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I like the monitoring. I like the reusable templates. That's the bit that speaks to our actual problem.
findings.context: Prospect values reusable templates/subflows as the feature that addresses their maintenance problem with many separate automations. — Vendor framed subflows as reducing ~60 Zaps to about eight; prospect called it the most compelling point and said templates speak to the actual problem.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: What about visibility of who owns what? Because the dead-employee problem is real.
findings.context: Prospect needs visibility of automation ownership and change history; the ownership problem is a stated concern. — Former employees own many of the 60+ Zapier automations; vendor offered version history and publish-role controls.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Owned by who?
findings.context: Prospect requires an exception queue with a team-based owner for incomplete order data. — Asked what happens with incomplete order data and who owns the exception; vendor described group routing.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.
findings.context: Customer wants a weekly digest of recurring support reasons with verifiable links to source tickets; a dev/prod separation is also wanted. — Marcus's long-standing request; he distrusts summaries he cannot verify. Vendor offered AI optional steps.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: SSO would be nice rather than mandatory
findings.context: Prospect requires SSO as nice-to-have rather than mandatory, plus a standard DPA and clarity on UK/EU data processing location. — Security requirements raised; vendor said EU residency is Enterprise-only and default region for Growth unconfirmed.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: the headline items are SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity options, disaster recovery documentation, penetration test material, and German or EU data residency.
findings.context: Prospect's governance function requires a long list of security and compliance capabilities including SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity, DR documentation, pen test material, and EU data residency. — Anika lists headline governance items she will formally send; treated as a requirement list, not yet a deal-blocker by itself.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: If your platform must call them over the internet, that is not possible for those systems.
findings.context: Prospect requires that systems not be exposed to the public internet, so the platform cannot call them directly over the internet; private/agent-based connectivity is required. — Stated as a hard constraint by policy and network design; Martin says this is the answer he wanted for private connectivity.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant.
findings.context: Prospect's top priority is deployment architecture and on-premise/SAP connectivity; it is the deciding factor before any product demo or pilot. — Martin says a product demo is irrelevant if deployment architecture fails; he asked to remove the demo from the agenda.

findings.speaker: Jon Bell
findings.quote: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise.
findings.context: Prospect requires SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning; OrbitFlow vendor says both are supported on Enterprise. — Vendor statement about its own product, not validated by customer.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: If business operations own workflows, business operations must not own credentials.
findings.context: Prospect requires that business operations not hold credentials; secrets must not appear in logs, and credentials should be centrally managed. — Governance concern raised by Anika; vendor says connections are centrally managed and secret values are not displayed in run logs.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: I want to see what happens when data is missing, when SAP does not respond, when an approver does nothing for two days, and when the account changes state after the workflow has already started.
findings.context: Prospect needs exception handling, approvals, and timeouts in workflows; the phase-one use case must handle missing data, SAP non-response, approver inaction, and mid-run contract amendments. — Martin emphasises edge cases over the happy path; vendor says these are patterns, not switches.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual?
findings.context: Prospect requires exception queues owned by teams rather than individuals, and wants audit data exportable to its own systems rather than a vendor console as the audit trail. — Anika cites individual ownership as a reason past automations decayed; she considers audit export satisfactory after vendor confirmed API/webhook export.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: My position is that I do not want generative AI in the first phase at all.
findings.context: Prospect will not accept generative AI in phase one; wants AI features disable-able and contractually guaranteed that workflow content is not used to train a shared model. — Anika's position; vendor says Enterprise can disable AI features and does not train on customer content.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test
findings.context: Prospect requires separate dev, test, and production workspaces with change control and separation of builder and approver; change-management scenarios (build, change, break, roll back) must be in evaluation. — Stated as non-negotiable; vendor says workspace separation is supported but promotion/rollback needs walkthrough.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: If a workflow monitors employee activity in any way
findings.context: Prospect wants team-level rather than individual-level visibility of workflow run durations to avoid works council co-determination issues. — Individual performance monitoring of employees triggers works council review, which may take about six months.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: It is not a tool that business operations should be using directly
findings.context: Prospect's key use case is business-owned workflow and approval layer above MuleSoft, not replacement of MuleSoft; first candidate is contract close to SAP validation to ServiceNow tasks. — Vendor and customer agree on positioning; MuleSoft is owned and seen as integration backbone.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: We are much worse at telling you why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same pattern occurred fifteen times last month.
findings.context: Prospect wants operational telemetry to diagnose stalls and which dependency failed, which it currently lacks. — Current visibility is weak; ask is for failure-reason and pattern reporting.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case.
findings.context: Prospect's SAP connectivity viability is the deciding question; the biggest risk is whether SAP and on-premise systems make phase one too heavy. — Martin frames this as the crux; the alternative is building on MuleSoft.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: The main gates are model-risk and auditability. If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Prospect's primary gates are model-risk governance and auditability; if these aren't satisfied, connector breadth won't save the project. — Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer) states the deal-blocking gates; Noah confirms auditability is the core problem.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: exportable audit history
findings.context: Prospect requires an exportable, programmatic audit history, specifically streamed into their SIEM, and needs audit export as a capability. — Hannah defines the requirement list; she accepts API/webhook export only after clarifying she means programmatic export, not a UI CSV.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
findings.context: Prospect's security/audit requirement list includes SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency, and contractual no-training language. — Hannah lists the auditability gate items; SSO/SCIM is named as a requirement.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
findings.context: Prospect's deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and a genuinely programmatic audit export; connector breadth is a tie. — Hannah answers Leo's direct question on what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Large visual workflows are hard for our people to reason about.
findings.context: Debugging large visual workflows is a major pain point; engineers struggle with failures deep in big flows, and the Tray PoC debugging experience was poor. — Noah relays Hannah's blunt criticism of Tray's debugging; Hannah later names debugging loop and error handling as the hardest part.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
findings.context: Prospect praises Tray's connector breadth, so connector breadth is not a differentiator or current complaint. — Noah's view of the Tray PoC; Hannah later calls connector breadth a tie.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, and an internal event bus. Required: all of those, plus webhooks and a generic REST connector.
findings.context: Required integrations are Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, and an internal event bus, plus webhooks and a generic REST connector. — Noah lists the stack requirements; the internal event bus (Kafka-based, not externally reachable) is flagged as an architecture challenge.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Is the original value retained?
findings.context: Prospect needs run history that records every step, inputs/outputs, retries, and human approvals, and needs to know whether original values are retained after human edits. — Hannah probes the failed-and-remediated run; the vendor clarifies retention depends on how the approval was configured.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Can you enforce that or is it a convention?
findings.context: Prospect needs guardrails against AI outputs feeding automated decisions; the vendor admits this is only a design convention, not an enforced platform constraint, and the prospect wants it recorded as a known limitation. — Model-risk concern; vendor disclosure of a real gap.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Can I have a workspace where they're disabled and another where they aren't?
findings.context: Prospect needs per-workspace control to disable AI features and restrict models. — Hannah asks for disabled and enabled workspaces side by side; vendor will confirm granularity in writing.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
findings.context: Prospect needs environment separation (dev/prod) and a change-management scenario covering build, change, break, and rollback. — Hannah insists on testing rollback, not just building.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named person?
findings.context: Prospect needs exception queues owned by a team rather than a named person, with an on-call style fallback and separate handling for operational incidents versus business exceptions. — Key-person dependency problem; Noah asks about PagerDuty integration.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Operational telemetry is weak
findings.context: Prospect wants operational telemetry on why exceptions happen and which dependency failed; current telemetry is weak. — Current state gap; outcome metrics exist but root-cause visibility does not.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Can I unit test a subflow?
findings.context: Prospect has a clear priority for composable subflows and unit-testable debugging; the vendor says subflow isolation is not a true unit test. — Composition was the vendor's answer to the debugging criticism; Hannah accepts isolated runs as most of what she wants.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
findings.context: Prospect's core concern with retries is idempotency: engineers could not tell whether a step had run twice under Tray. — Hannah names retry semantics as a Tray problem; vendor says design mitigation is required.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect wants predictable pricing with explicit overage and cap mechanisms, and a clear split of licensed builders versus approval-only users. — Commercial requirements; Noah worries about second-year overages; not a product feature per se but a stated must-have.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: reporting data gets manually copied between HubSpot and spreadsheets
findings.context: Prospect's core pain is manual copying of data between HubSpot and spreadsheets for reporting, which they want automated; they quantify it as a waste of time. — Pain point framing from the COO; reporting/data sync requirement

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Deal closes in HubSpot, we create the right Asana project from a template, assign the owners, spin up a Slack channel, chase whatever client information's missing, and alert me when a launch date slips.
findings.context: Prospect's required workflow: deal closes in HubSpot, auto-create Asana project from template, assign owners, create Slack channel, chase missing client info, and alert when a launch date slips. — Specific use-case requirement stated twice; treated as the must-have for evaluation

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I see it as useful but too fragile for multi-step onboarding — the minute there's a branch or something needs a person to do something, it falls over.
findings.context: Prospect's existing stack is HubSpot, Slack, Google Workspace, Asana and Google Sheets, and they already run about twenty Zapier Zaps that they find fragile for multi-step onboarding with branches or human steps. — Integration requirements and concern about Zapier limitations

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: And if nobody changes the record but the date just passes?
findings.context: Prospect needs the date-slip alert to fire even when no record changes (time-based trigger); vendor was unsure and said it would need an SE to confirm, possibly requiring two workflows. — Concern about event-driven vs scheduled checks; OrbitFlow's answer was uncertain

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
findings.context: Prospect needs an accurate weekly summary of overdue onboarding tasks; inaccurate AI output is considered worse than nothing. — Concern about AI summary accuracy; vendor deflected to checking underlying data

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: We'd want Google login or SAML, normal GDPR terms, and — this one matters — written reassurance that our client documents aren't used to train models.
findings.context: Prospect requires SSO via Google login or SAML and written assurance that client documents are not used to train AI models; vendor said SSO is included on all plans and asked to confirm; prospect doubts it is not enterprise-only. — Security requirements; prospect says other vendors gated SSO to enterprise

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: each client-services pod is intentionally allowed to customise parts of it. That's not an accident, it's how we work.
findings.context: Prospect's team wants to customise onboarding per client-services pod; a standardised workflow would meet resistance, and vendor claimed full flexibility. — Requirement for per-pod configurability; vendor claimed it was just configuration

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all. An operations manager would administer this.
findings.context: Prospect has no IT team; the operations manager would administer the tool, so it must be genuinely no-code. Vendor said it is completely no-code. — Usability requirement given lack of technical staff

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
findings.context: Prospect is not interested in governance/audit trail features as a justification; they do not see a need for auditing their onboarding. — Prospect pushback on vendor's differentiator (governance, visibility, audit trail)

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: But supervisors still coordinate the remediation through phone calls and spreadsheets.
findings.context: Prospect's most important capability need is coordination of remediation work, not visibility: they want the workflow to move blocked installations along, with Dynamics kept current as the issue changes state. — Customer-stated priority; the candidate workflow was offered by vendor and accepted by customer as the right one.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
findings.context: Dynamics 365 integration is a mandatory requirement and the prospect calls the lack of a first-class Dynamics connector the biggest issue for them. — Vendor admitted no deepest first-class Dynamics connector; customer said it is the decisive gap versus embedded Power Automate.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: And this is the thing that kills most vendors.
findings.context: Offline / intermittent connectivity tolerance is a hard constraint: workflows cannot assume mobile devices are online, and the absence of a sync signal should be treated as an exception. — Customer raised field connectivity; vendor proposed sync-event trigger and timeout branch; customer agreed absence of signal is important.

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: If a regional supervisor can look at a failed thing and understand what happened without raising a ticket to Carlos's team, that's material.
findings.context: Troubleshooting/debuggability by regional supervisors without raising tickets is what would make OrbitFlow materially better; reusability of remediation patterns across regions is also a stated priority. — Customer's definition of 'materially better' in response to vendor question.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Azure AD SSO, audit logs, preferably UK data residency, and controls that let us limit access by region.
findings.context: Security requirements: Azure AD SSO, audit logs, preferred UK data residency, and region-level access control; customer says residency is preferred not mandatory. — Vendor confirmed SAML SSO/SCIM on Enterprise and EU residency, UK unconfirmed; customer clarified preference not regulatory requirement.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Can the queue be owned by a team? Because our supervisors rotate and if it's assigned to a person, that person's on leave.
findings.context: Customer needs a complex-flow troubleshooting and ownership capability; queues must be team-owned and on-call resolvable because supervisors rotate, with rota currently split between Dynamics and a shared calendar. — Customer's requirements for exception routing and on-call; not a fully stated deal-breaker.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: That's more or less what I'd want.
findings.context: Regional self-service building with central governance is valued: two regions already build their own Power Automate flows and the prospect wants regional workspaces with controlled promotion. — Customer correction of earlier statement that regions cannot maintain automations; interest in regional workspace separation.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Power Automate is the incumbent and a strong competitor; the prospect's requirement is that OrbitFlow be materially better, and they want a side-by-side test against it. — Customer states Power Automate is embedded and approved; vendor proposed benchmark.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: Conflicts is not negotiable. If a workflow makes a conflicts decision, we're finished.
findings.context: Prospect requires that the workflow have no write path to the conflicts system, enforced at the permission/credential level rather than by design choice. — Security constraint named as non-negotiable; prospect wants it as a design constraint.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Can I audit that? Can I see which connections a workflow uses?
findings.context: Prospect wants to audit which connections a workflow uses and to review connection scopes as a standing control. — Security/audit capability; vendor recommended reviewing connection scopes instead of workflows, prospect agreed it was better.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: The "pass references rather than payloads" principle is the one I care about. Can you actually build that way?
findings.context: Prospect needs field/payload-level protection: wants workflows to pass references rather than sensitive payloads, since run history exposes whatever data is passed. — Concern about matter data visible in run history; vendor said no field-level masking switch exists, only design patterns.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: Yes. This is the big one. We have matters where the team acting for one side must not be able to see anything relating to the other.

draft.answer: Across all 10 prospect calls, the most consistent capability priorities were observability and debuggable run history [C1], team-owned exception queues [C2], and robust handling of failures and messy data [C3]. Prospects also repeatedly required audit export to their own systems [C4], version history and change control [C5], and tight controls on AI, often switched off in phase one [C6]. Reliable integrations with specific systems, reusable subflows, governance and permissions, and data residency were also named [C7][C8][C9]. Connector breadth was not a differentiator for Ember [C10].

claims.text: Observability, run history and debugging were a recurring top need: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan), BrightPath Health (Priya Shah), DeltaWorks (Martin Vogel) and Ember Financial (Noah Williams) each said current telemetry is weak and they cannot see why or which dependency failed. BrightPath asked to see a failed run. Ember's Hannah Cole said debugging and audit trail decide OrbitFlow vs Tray. Greenline wants supervisors to understand failures without raising a ticket, and Harbor Legal's Eleanor Brooks named monitoring as missing from Power Automate. Acme also wants metrics exported to its own monitoring.

Exception queues owned by a team rather than a named person were requested by Acme, BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Greenline. Reasons given include staff turnover, supervisors rotating, and departed employees owning automations.

Prospects want workflows tested on failure paths, not just the happy path (missing data, API timeouts, approver inaction, mid-run state changes): Acme, BrightPath and DeltaWorks. Related asks were schema-change and bad-data alerting (Acme, BrightPath), failure-rate alerting (Cedar & Finch), idempotent retry semantics (Ember), and offline/intermittent connectivity tolerance (Greenline).

Exportable audit logs for the prospect's own systems were required by BrightPath (SIEM), DeltaWorks, Ember (programmatic SIEM export) and Harbor Legal, each saying console-only logs are not an audit trail. Ember named auditability and model-risk as its primary gates. SSO/SCIM and audit logs were also commonly listed as baseline security requirements, though Acme said these are part of the usual review rather than a deal gate and Cedar & Finch called SSO nice-to-have.

Version history, change visibility and change-management scenarios were required by Acme, BrightPath, Ember (build, change, break, roll back) and DeltaWorks (separate dev/test/prod, called non-negotiable). Inkwell and Juniper want workflow logic reviewable or diffable in version control.

AI controls matter: Acme, Ember, Harbor Legal, BrightPath and DeltaWorks want AI disable-able (per workspace or off for phase one), and several want contractual no-training language. BrightPath and DeltaWorks will not accept AI in phase one. Inkwell, Cedar & Finch and Fable want AI summaries to be verifiable/accurate with links to source tickets, and Inkwell wants AI to be able to say it doesn't know. Acme is wary of agentic AI. Ember wants guardrails on AI feeding decisions, which the vendor admitted is only a convention.

Integration reliability and specific connectors were top priorities: the system-of-record connector is a deal-breaker for Acme (Salesforce) and BrightPath. Cedar & Finch requires a native event-driven Shopify trigger. Greenline calls the lack of a first-class Dynamics 365 connector its biggest issue. DeltaWorks' deciding factor is SAP/on-premise private connectivity. Harbor Legal wants iManage/Intapp integrations, which are limited. Juniper worries about Salesforce API limits and the Postgres connector.

Reusable components/subflows were valued by BrightPath (backlog answer), Cedar & Finch (most compelling point), Greenline, Harbor Legal and Ember (unit-testable subflows). Prospects also want business-ops self-service with engineering-governed connectors and credentials (Juniper, DeltaWorks, Fable's no-code need), and centrally managed secrets (Acme, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal, Juniper).

Fine-grained data protection and residency appeared in several security-led calls. Field-level masking was wanted by Acme, BrightPath and Harbor Legal (the vendor said it is design-based, not a switch). Harbor Legal needs matter-level ethical walls, which the vendor lacks natively. Residency needs: UK for Harbor Legal (unconfirmed), EU for Juniper, Ember and DeltaWorks, UK preferred for Greenline.
Ember said connector breadth is a tie with Tray rather than a differentiator. Fable Media said it did not value governance or audit-trail features, so priorities vary by prospect.

claims.text: AI controls matter: Acme, Ember, Harbor Legal, BrightPath and DeltaWorks want AI disable-able (per workspace or off for phase one), and several want contractual no-training language. BrightPath and DeltaWorks will not accept AI in phase one. Inkwell, Cedar & Finch and Fable want AI summaries to be verifiable/accurate with links to source tickets, and Inkwell wants AI to be able to say it doesn't know. Acme is wary of agentic AI. Ember wants guardrails on AI feeding decisions, which the vendor admitted is only a convention.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: Can we see the prompt and the model config? And can we switch AI off entirely for a workspace?
evidence.context: Prospect wants controls on AI: ability to inspect prompts and model config, disable AI per workspace, and a written commitment that customer data is not used for training. — AI capability concerns; OrbitFlow said data is not used for training and this belongs in the contract.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Can I have a workspace where they're disabled and another where they aren't?
evidence.context: Prospect needs per-workspace control to disable AI features and restrict models. — Hannah asks for disabled and enabled workspaces side by side; vendor will confirm granularity in writing.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: Off. For phase one, off.
evidence.context: Prospect requires the ability to disable AI features entirely for phase one. — AI-off is a stated phase-one requirement; the sponsor has a separate AI use case for later.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: What happens to data sent to an LLM provider?
evidence.context: Prospect requires that the AI/LLM feature not be used for phase one; AI steps are acceptable only as a separately reviewed later phase, and the no-training-on-customer-data commitment must be in the contract. — Security concern about LLM provider data handling; prospect accepts deferring AI.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: My position is that I do not want generative AI in the first phase at all.
evidence.context: Prospect will not accept generative AI in phase one; wants AI features disable-able and contractually guaranteed that workflow content is not used to train a shared model. — Anika's position; vendor says Enterprise can disable AI features and does not train on customer content.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
evidence.context: Prospect wants a weekly narrative summary whose claims link back to the supporting tickets, rather than an unverifiable output. — Requirement for the AI summary feature. Olivia currently receives a spreadsheet she does not read.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: Can it say "I don't know"? If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
evidence.context: Prospect asks whether the AI summary can say it has no finding, and wants thin evidence to be refused rather than invented. — Concern about the model inventing themes; vendor says the workflow should enforce minimum evidence rather than rely on model confidence.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Lee
evidence.quote: With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.
evidence.context: Customer wants a weekly digest of recurring support reasons with verifiable links to source tickets; a dev/prod separation is also wanted. — Marcus's long-standing request; he distrusts summaries he cannot verify. Vendor offered AI optional steps.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
evidence.context: Prospect needs an accurate weekly summary of overdue onboarding tasks; inaccurate AI output is considered worse than nothing. — Concern about AI summary accuracy; vendor deflected to checking underlying data

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of agentic AI and prefers deterministic rules for high-stakes steps; AI should be optional and explainable. — Concern about explainability of AI features.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Can you enforce that or is it a convention?
evidence.context: Prospect needs guardrails against AI outputs feeding automated decisions; the vendor admits this is only a design convention, not an enforced platform constraint, and the prospect wants it recorded as a known limitation. — Model-risk concern; vendor disclosure of a real gap.

claims.text: Integration reliability and specific connectors were top priorities: the system-of-record connector is a deal-breaker for Acme (Salesforce) and BrightPath. Cedar & Finch requires a native event-driven Shopify trigger. Greenline calls the lack of a first-class Dynamics 365 connector its biggest issue. DeltaWorks' deciding factor is SAP/on-premise private connectivity. Harbor Legal wants iManage/Intapp integrations, which are limited. Juniper worries about Salesforce API limits and the Postgres connector.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable, none of the rest matters. After that it's the collaboration and data systems, because that's where context goes missing.
evidence.context: Salesforce connector reliability is the deal-breaker; Slack and data systems matter next for phase one; Gainsight is useful but not essential. — Integration priority ranking in response to OrbitFlow's question.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: The system of record. If that connector's unreliable none of the rest matters.
evidence.context: Prospect's phase-one use case needs integrations with HubSpot, Microsoft Teams, Jira Service Management, and Azure AD; Databricks is API-only and not phase one. The system of record connector is the deal-breaker. — Integration priorities; prospect says reliability of the system-of-record connector matters most.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Shopify. A native Shopify trigger is — that's important. If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Prospect's most important integration is Shopify; she requires a native, event-driven Shopify trigger and rejects polling. — Prospect names Shopify as the one that 'has to work perfectly'; vendor declined to confirm trigger coverage and promised a written answer.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us.
evidence.context: Dynamics 365 integration is a mandatory requirement and the prospect calls the lack of a first-class Dynamics connector the biggest issue for them. — Vendor admitted no deepest first-class Dynamics connector; customer said it is the decisive gap versus embedded Power Automate.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant.
evidence.context: Prospect's top priority is deployment architecture and on-premise/SAP connectivity; it is the deciding factor before any product demo or pilot. — Martin says a product demo is irrelevant if deployment architecture fails; he asked to remove the demo from the agenda.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: If your platform must call them over the internet, that is not possible for those systems.
evidence.context: Prospect requires that systems not be exposed to the public internet, so the platform cannot call them directly over the internet; private/agent-based connectivity is required. — Stated as a hard constraint by policy and network design; Martin says this is the answer he wanted for private connectivity.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Prospect requires native or well-maintained integrations with iManage and Intapp; vendor says native legal-system connectors are limited and would be API-based integration work. — Integration effort is the prospect's main reservation about value versus cost.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Salesforce API limits are the constraint. We've hit them before.
evidence.context: Prospect is concerned about Salesforce API rate limits, which they have hit before, and needs the design to fit their daily allocation. — Integration constraint; vendor asked for the number.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I care about webhooks, REST, and whether the Postgres connector does anything stupid.
evidence.context: Prospect requires the Postgres connector to handle connections and timeouts safely and not run unbounded queries against production. — Technical concern about connector behaviour; vendor recommended a read replica.

claims.text: Reusable components/subflows were valued by BrightPath (backlog answer), Cedar & Finch (most compelling point), Greenline, Harbor Legal and Ember (unit-testable subflows). Prospects also want business-ops self-service with engineering-governed connectors and credentials (Juniper, DeltaWorks, Fable's no-code need), and centrally managed secrets (Acme, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal, Juniper).

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: That's the backlog answer, potentially.
evidence.context: Prospect wants reusable components so the systems group builds subflows and business users assemble workflows, reducing the request backlog. — Prospect sees this as the backlog answer; vendor says it compounds over time.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: I like the monitoring. I like the reusable templates. That's the bit that speaks to our actual problem.
evidence.context: Prospect values reusable templates/subflows as the feature that addresses their maintenance problem with many separate automations. — Vendor framed subflows as reducing ~60 Zaps to about eight; prospect called it the most compelling point and said templates speak to the actual problem.

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: If a regional supervisor can look at a failed thing and understand what happened without raising a ticket to Carlos's team, that's material.
evidence.context: Troubleshooting/debuggability by regional supervisors without raising tickets is what would make OrbitFlow materially better; reusability of remediation patterns across regions is also a stated priority. — Customer's definition of 'materially better' in response to vendor question.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: Monitoring, mostly. And reusable components.
evidence.context: Prospect's current incumbent Power Automate is missing monitoring and reusable components; these are the desired capabilities. — Pain points with incumbent tool.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Can I unit test a subflow?
evidence.context: Prospect has a clear priority for composable subflows and unit-testable debugging; the vendor says subflow isolation is not a true unit test. — Composition was the vendor's answer to the debugging criticism; Hannah accepts isolated runs as most of what she wants.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I'm not fine with production connector code and secrets sitting outside engineering review.
evidence.context: Prospect wants a split: business logic owned by business operations in the UI, while connector code and credentials are engineering-owned and reviewed. — Core requirement agreed on the call and written down by the vendor as a requirement.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: the thing that actually costs us is that business teams depend on engineers to change even small rules.
evidence.context: Prospect's key business problem: business rule changes wait in the engineering queue; a simple threshold change took eleven days. — Driver for the business-ops self-service requirement.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all. An operations manager would administer this.
evidence.context: Prospect has no IT team; the operations manager would administer the tool, so it must be genuinely no-code. Vendor said it is completely no-code. — Usability requirement given lack of technical staff

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: If business operations own workflows, business operations must not own credentials.
evidence.context: Prospect requires that business operations not hold credentials; secrets must not appear in logs, and credentials should be centrally managed. — Governance concern raised by Anika; vendor says connections are centrally managed and secret values are not displayed in run logs.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: Can secrets be rotated without editing every workflow?
evidence.context: Prospect wants workflows to call internal APIs and rotate secrets centrally without editing every workflow. — Technical integration questions asked near end of call.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: Can secrets be rotated without editing every workflow?
evidence.context: Prospect wants secrets rotatable without editing every workflow and wants clarity on data handling at termination. — Technical security questions asked before close.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Who can create a connection?
evidence.context: Prospect requires secrets and production credentials to be centrally governed, with the ability to scope connection creation to engineering. — Security/least-privilege requirement; vendor confirmed connections are centrally managed.

claims.text: Fine-grained data protection and residency appeared in several security-led calls. Field-level masking was wanted by Acme, BrightPath and Harbor Legal (the vendor said it is design-based, not a switch). Harbor Legal needs matter-level ethical walls, which the vendor lacks natively. Residency needs: UK for Harbor Legal (unconfirmed), EU for Juniper, Ember and DeltaWorks, UK preferred for Greenline.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: We'll have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without necessarily seeing all the customer data in it.
evidence.context: Prospect requires permission separation so admins can see step failures without seeing all customer payload data. — Field-level access concern; OrbitFlow said exact field masking should be part of security design.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
evidence.context: Prospect needs field-level masking so admins can see a step failed without seeing record contents; vendor says this is designable, not a standard checkbox. — Run-data visibility concern; vendor declined to promise it as a yes.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: The "pass references rather than payloads" principle is the one I care about. Can you actually build that way?
evidence.context: Prospect needs field/payload-level protection: wants workflows to pass references rather than sensitive payloads, since run history exposes whatever data is passed. — Concern about matter data visible in run history; vendor said no field-level masking switch exists, only design patterns.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: Yes. This is the big one. We have matters where the team acting for one side must not be able to see anything relating to the other.
evidence.context: Matter-level information barriers (ethical walls) are a major requirement; prospect says nobody has answered well whether a workflow platform can respect them. Vendor states no native matter-level ethical wall exists. — Vendor admitted a capability gap; prospect scoped phase one to barrier-free matters.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: UK residency?
evidence.context: Prospect requires UK data residency; EU residency is available on Enterprise but UK is unconfirmed and may be a deal gate. — Vendor could not confirm UK specifically; important for public sector clients.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
evidence.context: Prospect needs EU data residency because of data residency commitments in some enterprise contracts. — Customer confirmed two enterprise contracts; may be more unknown.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
evidence.context: Prospect's security/audit requirement list includes SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency, and contractual no-training language. — Hannah lists the auditability gate items; SSO/SCIM is named as a requirement.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: the headline items are SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity options, disaster recovery documentation, penetration test material, and German or EU data residency.
evidence.context: Prospect's governance function requires a long list of security and compliance capabilities including SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity, DR documentation, pen test material, and EU data residency. — Anika lists headline governance items she will formally send; treated as a requirement list, not yet a deal-blocker by itself.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Azure AD SSO, audit logs, preferably UK data residency, and controls that let us limit access by region.
evidence.context: Security requirements: Azure AD SSO, audit logs, preferred UK data residency, and region-level access control; customer says residency is preferred not mandatory. — Vendor confirmed SAML SSO/SCIM on Enterprise and EU residency, UK unconfirmed; customer clarified preference not regulatory requirement.

claims.text: Ember said connector breadth is a tie with Tray rather than a differentiator. Fable Media said it did not value governance or audit-trail features, so priorities vary by prospect.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
evidence.context: Prospect's deciding factors versus Tray are debugging experience and a genuinely programmatic audit export; connector breadth is a tie. — Hannah answers Leo's direct question on what must be true to choose OrbitFlow over Tray.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Connector breadth is genuinely good. No complaints there.
evidence.context: Prospect praises Tray's connector breadth, so connector breadth is not a differentiator or current complaint. — Noah's view of the Tray PoC; Hannah later calls connector breadth a tie.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
evidence.context: Prospect is not interested in governance/audit trail features as a justification; they do not see a need for auditing their onboarding. — Prospect pushback on vendor's differentiator (governance, visibility, audit trail)

conflicts.description: Fable Media's COO said no one audits their onboarding, whereas BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Ember and Harbor Legal treated audit export as a gate or key requirement.

conflicts.topic: Importance of SSO/security as a gate
conflicts.description: Acme said SSO and audit logs are part of a usual review and not a deal gate, and Cedar & Finch called SSO nice-to-have. BrightPath, DeltaWorks and Ember list SSO/SCIM among formal requirements.

Whether any of these capabilities actually decided a deal outcome.

No specific company named, so companies is empty.
